reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / KDIGO
clinicalPearls: RTA produces a normal anion gap (hyperchloraemic) metabolic acidosis despite relatively preserved glomerular filtration, distinguishing it from the high anion gap acidosis of advanced renal failure

Type 1 (distal) RTA reflects failure of the distal nephron to secrete hydrogen ions, so urine pH stays inappropriately high (typically above 5.5) in the face of systemic acidosis, and is usually accompanied by hypokalaemia
Type 2 (proximal) RTA arises from impaired proximal reabsorption of bicarbonate; once serum bicarbonate falls below the lowered threshold, distal acidification can still generate acidic urine
Type 4 RTA is a hyperkalaemic form driven by aldosterone deficiency or resistance, most commonly seen in diabetic kidney disease, and impairs both acid and potassium excretion
Nephrocalcinosis and calcium-containing stones are characteristic of distal RTA because of hypercalciuria, low urinary citrate, and alkaline urine

The urine anion gap is a useful bedside tool: a positive (or inappropriately non-negative) value in the presence of acidosis points to impaired renal ammonium excretion rather than gastrointestinal bicarbonate loss
Proximal RTA frequently coexists with generalised proximal tubular dysfunction (Fanconi syndrome), so glycosuria, phosphaturia, and aminoaciduria should be sought

Management principles centre on alkali replacement; distal RTA usually needs modest alkali plus potassium, while proximal RTA requires larger alkali loads and often potassium supplementation because bicarbonate therapy worsens kaliuresis
reference.pathophysiology: The renal tubular acidoses are disorders in which the kidney fails to appropriately acidify the urine or reclaim filtered bicarbonate despite normal or near-normal glomerular filtration, producing a hyperchloraemic (normal anion gap) metabolic acidosis. In distal (type 1) RTA the collecting duct cannot secrete hydrogen ions effectively, so net acid excretion falls and the urine cannot be maximally acidified. In proximal (type 2) RTA the proximal tubule cannot reabsorb the filtered bicarbonate load, leading to bicarbonate wasting until serum levels reach a new lower steady state. Type 4 RTA results from deficient or ineffective aldosterone action, reducing distal sodium reabsorption and potassium and hydrogen secretion, which produces hyperkalaemia and a mild acidosis. Potassium behaves differently across subtypes: distal and proximal forms tend toward hypokalaemia, whereas the aldosterone-related form causes hyperkalaemia.
additionalDifferentials: Diarrhoea and other gastrointestinal bicarbonate losses
Early or advanced chronic kidney disease with reduced ammoniagenesis
Carbonic anhydrase inhibitor or other drug effect
Dilutional acidosis from rapid saline infusion
Addison disease or hypoaldosteronism from other causes
additionalInvestigations: Serum electrolytes with calculation of the plasma anion gap to confirm a normal-gap acidosis
Simultaneous urine pH and urine electrolytes to calculate the urine anion gap and assess ammonium excretion
Serum potassium to help classify the subtype (low in types 1 and 2, high in type 4)
Urinalysis for glycosuria, proteinuria, and evidence of proximal tubular dysfunction
Renal imaging for nephrocalcinosis or stones, especially in distal RTA
Plasma renin and aldosterone when a hyperkalaemic (type 4) picture is suspected
redFlags: Severe hypokalaemia causing muscle weakness, paralysis, or arrhythmia in distal or proximal RTA
Dangerous hyperkalaemia in type 4 RTA, particularly with concurrent potassium-retaining drugs
Growth failure, rickets, or osteomalacia in children and adults from chronic acidosis and phosphate loss
Recurrent stones or progressive nephrocalcinosis threatening renal function
reference.prognosis: With appropriate alkali and electrolyte correction most patients do well, and complications such as bone disease, stones, and growth impairment can be prevented or limited. Outcome depends heavily on the underlying cause; type 4 RTA linked to diabetic nephropathy tends to progress with the primary kidney disease, while inherited distal RTA requires lifelong therapy.
pitfalls: Attributing a normal anion gap acidosis to diarrhoea without checking the urine anion gap or urine ammonium
Giving bicarbonate in proximal RTA without adequate potassium, precipitating worsening hypokalaemia
Overlooking type 4 RTA as a cause of unexplained hyperkalaemia in a diabetic patient
Failing to search for Fanconi syndrome features when proximal RTA is diagnosed
Assuming a high urine pH always indicates distal RTA without excluding urinary infection with urea-splitting organisms
management: Correct the metabolic acidosis with oral alkali therapy, choosing potassium citrate or sodium bicarbonate according to subtype
In distal (type 1) RTA use potassium citrate to correct acidosis and hypokalaemia while reducing hypercalciuria, low citrate and stone formation
In proximal (type 2) RTA give abundant alkali replacement with potassium supplementation, and consider a thiazide to reduce bicarbonate wasting

In hyperkalaemic (type 4) RTA restrict dietary potassium, add a loop diuretic or fludrocortisone, and withdraw drugs that worsen hyperkalaemia such as renin-angiotensin blockers and potassium-sparing diuretics
Identify and treat any underlying cause such as autoimmune disease, drugs or obstructive uropathy
Monitor electrolytes and acid-base status, screen for nephrocalcinosis and stones, and follow growth in children

valueTables.title: Causes of non-anion gap acidosis

cells.text: Diarrhea; external pancreatic or small-bowel drainage; ureterosigmoidostomy, jejunal loop, ileal loop; drugs: calcium chloride (acidifying agent), magnesium sulfate (diarrhea), cholestyramine (bile acid diarrhea)
Proximal RTA (type 2), drug-induced: acetazolamide, topiramate; distal (classic) RTA (type 1), drug-induced: amphotericin B, ifosfamide

Generalized distal nephron dysfunction (type 4 RTA): mineralocorticoid deficiency; mineralocorticoid resistance (autosomal dominant PHA I); voltage defect (autosomal dominant PHA I and PHA II); tubulointerstitial disease
Potassium-sparing diuretics (amiloride, triamterene, spironolactone); trimethoprim; pentamidine; ACE inhibitors and ARBs; nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs; cyclosporine and tacrolimus
Acid loads (ammonium chloride, hyperalimentation); loss of potential bicarbonate (ketosis with ketone excretion); expansion acidosis (rapid saline administration); hippurate; cation exchange resins
